chapter: Lu Barker and the Barbarin family
title: Radio would not play the risque records and wanted no ballads
summary: Milt and Danny say stations banned suggestive records, and Lu's ballads were turned down for record dates.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: You see, the people in New York, they weren't hip to that. See, Blues or... Now they're just beginning to get wise to Folk music.
And they wouldn't even play one of those records on the air.

Look at what they're doing on television now. And they wouldn't play those records, those albums... Now they have sex openly on the screen, and they wouldn't play a record that suggested it even then! Times sure have
And I could sing in those days beautiful ballads. But they didn't want no ballads.
Well, we was featuring ballads on the job, but not, you know, for the studios -- they didn't want that. For the records.

Oh, I couldn't sing that. I'd sing 'Music, Maestro, Please,' 'The Masquerade Is Over.' See, I'd mix them up, because I could sing the hot tunes, I could sing a ballad and I could sing a Blues, you know. You could do it on a job, you know.
But when you'd do it to make a record, everybody wanted to...
